family.name: K5 Blazer & Suburban
family.verdict: General Motors took a half-ton pickup, cut a bit off the back and made the roof optional, and the Bronco and Scout never quite recovered. Then it did the opposite with the Suburban, giving it nine seats and four doors. Neither one is subtle, and both are easy to keep running.
intro: Chevrolet came late to the off-road wagon fight. Ford had the Bronco and International had the Scout, so for 1969 Chevrolet shortened its K10 half-ton pickup from a 115-inch to a 104-inch wheelbase and called the result the K5 Blazer. It was bigger than both rivals, with a removable top, an optional passenger seat and the same engines and parts as the pickup. By 1970 it was outselling them. That year GMC also started selling it as the GMC Jimmy.

The first trucks, the [[chevrolet/k5-blazer-1st|1969–72 K5 Blazer]], had a full-length lift-off top. For 1973 GM moved to the 'Rounded Line' platform that enthusiasts call the square body. The [[chevrolet/k5-blazer|1973–91 K5 Blazer]] got a half-cab body in 1976, small-block V8s, a 6.2-liter diesel from 1982 and a military version, the M1009. Its rear roof still came off right up to 1991.

The [[chevrolet/suburban-square|1973–91 Suburban]] was built on the same chassis as a truck-based station wagon with four doors and up to nine seats. Chevrolet and GMC both sold it under the Suburban name. For 1992 the whole family moved to the GMT400 platform. The Jimmy became the GMC Yukon, and the full-size Blazer later became the Tahoe.

page.title: Chevrolet K5 Blazer (1973–1991)
page.eyebrow: CHEVROLET K5 BLAZER · GMC JIMMY · SQUARE BODY · 1973–1991
page.verdict: It's a half-ton pickup with the back seat where the bed should be and a roof you can unbolt. It has a small-block V8 you can fix with a wrench, axles that half the junkyard will fit, and a frame that cracks at the steering box. Owners love it anyway, and it's one of the easiest classic 4x4s to keep on the trail.

paragraphs: For 1973 General Motors redesigned its whole light-truck line. GM called it the 'Rounded Line', but everyone else calls it the square body, and the K5 Blazer came along with it. The formula stayed the same: take a four-wheel-drive half-ton pickup, shorten it, and make the roof removable. The new Blazer was 7 inches longer than the [[chevrolet/k5-blazer-1st|first generation]] on a wheelbase 2.5 inches longer. It stayed in production for 19 model years, through two facelifts, a diesel and an Army contract. GMC sold the same truck as the Jimmy, and the long-wheelbase [[chevrolet/suburban-square|Suburban]] as the GMC Suburban.

story.heading: A PICKUP WITH THE ROOF OPTIONAL
paragraphs: The K5 was built as an answer to the [[scout/scout-80-800|International Scout]] and the [[bronco/early-bronco|Ford Bronco]]. Because it shared its platform with the C/K pickups, it was bigger, roomier and more stable on the road than either. It also cost less to build, and buyers could add pickup options such as automatic transmissions, air conditioning and radios. By 1970 it was outselling its rivals. Rivals soon copied the idea. Jeep shortened its Gladiator into the [[jeep/sj-wagoneer|Cherokee]] for 1974, and Ford moved the [[bronco/full-size|Bronco onto the F-100 platform]] for 1978.

From 1973 to 1975 the Blazer was a fully open truck behind the windshield, with a choice of a removable hardtop or a convertible top. In 1976 GM made it a half-cab: a fixed steel roof over the front seats, which improved rollover protection and shared more parts with the pickups, and a removable fiberglass top over the back. That rear top still came off in 1991. The tailgate had a glass window that wound down inside it, either by hand crank or by an electric motor. The motor is a known weak point, so many of these windows no longer work.

story.heading: SMALL BLOCKS, ONE DIESEL AND FOUR TRANSFER CASES
paragraphs: The 250 straight-six was the base engine until 1982. Most buyers chose a small-block V8: a 307, 305 or 350, or from 1975 a 400. In 1973 Popular Science tested a 175 hp 350 automatic with full-time 4WD. It took 22.5 seconds to reach 60 mph, and the testers recorded 9.6 mpg at a steady 45 mph. For 1982 GM added a 6.2-liter diesel V8 developed with Detroit Diesel. It made 130 hp and 240 lb-ft at launch and fit the same mounts as the gas V8. In 1987 throttle-body injection arrived, and after that the TBI 350 was the standard engine.

Transfer cases tell you the truck's age. From 1973 to 1980 you got either the gear-driven, part-time NP205 or the chain-driven, full-time NP203 with a lockable center differential. GM dropped full-time 4WD after 1979. For 1981 the aluminum NP208 arrived, a part-time case you could shift into 4WD at up to 25 mph, along with automatic locking hubs. From 1989 the NP241 replaced it. Up front, early trucks had a Dana 44, and GM switched to its own corporate 10-bolt from 1977. The rear axle was a 12-bolt, then a 10-bolt. A full-floating 14-bolt from a three-quarter-ton truck is the swap owners usually make.

story.heading: SILVERADO, CHEYENNE AND THE ARMY
paragraphs: Trim levels followed the pickups. Custom Deluxe was the base model. Cheyenne added carpet, a headliner and extra insulation, and from 1975 Silverado was the top trim. Cheyenne trucks are usually 1970s models, because the name was dropped after 1981 and came back as a lower trim on the 1989–91 R/V trucks. Silverado ran to the end. GMC's Jimmy used Sierra names. In 1976 and 1977 a camper conversion was also offered: about 1,800 Blazer Chalet and Jimmy Casa Grande trucks with a pop-up camper body built by Chinook.

Then the Army bought some. Between 1983 and 1987 GM built the M1009, a K5 rated at three-quarter-ton capacity, as part of its Commercial Utility Cargo Vehicle program. It used the 6.2 diesel, a TH400 automatic and an NP208 transfer case. GM built about 70,000 CUCVs of all types, and many have since gone through government surplus sales. Some were replaced by the [[hummer/h1|Humvees]] they had been bought to supplement. Ex-military M1009s now come up for sale regularly, and one sold on Bring a Trailer for $20,500 in 2026.

story.heading: HOW IT ENDED
paragraphs: When the smaller S-10 Blazer appeared in 1983, GM officially renamed the big one the 'Full-Size Blazer' and the GMC version the 'K-Jimmy'. For 1987 the old trucks were renamed the R/V series, because the new GMT400 pickups took over the C/K name, and the Jimmy became the V-Jimmy. The Blazer, Suburban and crew cabs stayed on the old chassis. In 1988 the K5 badges disappeared. The 1989 trucks got a flatter grille in the style of the GMT400, plus the NP241 and 30-spline 10-bolt axle shafts. Rear anti-lock brakes and double-sided galvanized panels arrived for 1990.

1991 was the last year. The 1992 replacement moved to the GMT400 platform with a fixed roof, the Jimmy became the GMC Yukon, and in 1995 the full-size Blazer was renamed Tahoe. The square-body K5 is now an affordable classic that's very easy to modify. On Bring a Trailer, stock trucks often sell for less than $30,000, while LS-swapped restomods have reached six figures.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE ARMY BLAZER
callout.title: M1009 CUCV: a K5 with a 24-volt system
paragraphs: Around 1976 Vic Hickey, known as the father of the Humvee, used a K5 as a test vehicle for what became the CUCV program. The production M1009 had no air conditioning, an extra leaf in the springs, blackout lights, a brush guard, a rifle rack and paint in olive drab, woodland camouflage or desert tan. It ran on 10.00-15 tires and 3.08 gears, with open 10-bolt axles front and rear except for an Eaton automatic locker in the rear. It was rated for 1,200 lb of payload and a 3,000 lb towed load.

The odd part is the electrics. Two 12-volt alternators and two batteries are wired in series. The starter, the injection pump, the glow-plug circuit and the NATO slave receptacle use 24 volts, and everything else uses 12. The glow plugs are actually 12-volt plugs fed through a resistor pack on the firewall. Many civilian owners bypass the pack, fit a 12-volt starter and remove the second alternator.

page.engineering_intro: Mechanically, the square-body K5 is a shortened K10 pickup. It has a ladder frame, leaf springs and live axles at both ends, a transfer case bolted straight to the transmission, and the driveline mounted high to clear obstacles. Most parts are shared with GM's light trucks, which is why they're still easy to find. The details changed a lot over 19 years, so identify the axles and transfer case before you buy parts.

buying_checks.head: Frame cracks at the steering box
buying_checks.body: This is the classic K5 fault. On CK5 and GMSquareBody, owners say the frame cracks around and behind the steering-box bolts, often on the inside of the rail. You may not see the cracks with the box bolted on. Unbolt it if you can, or have someone rock the steering wheel while you watch for the frame moving. A properly welded reinforcement plate is fine; a bolt-on brace over an old crack isn't a fix.

buying_checks.head: Rust in the usual places
buying_checks.body: CK5 members list the rockers, the front floor and the front seat-belt anchors, the rear wheel arches, the tail pan, the bottoms of the doors and tailgate, the cab mounts and the rear floor supports by the tailgate hinges. Pull up the carpet and smell for mildew. If the paint is bubbling from outside, the rust underneath is usually already serious.

buying_checks.head: Tailgate window and top seal
buying_checks.body: Try the rear window. It winds down inside the tailgate by crank or motor, the motor and its drive cable are known to fail, and a safety switch stops the glass going up if the tailgate isn't latched. Ask whether the top has been removed. Owners disagree on whether that always causes leaks, but the seal between the top and the body is the usual leak point.

buying_checks.head: Is it really a 350?
buying_checks.body: One CK5 member warns about 305s being sold as 350s, engines described as 'rebuilt' that never were, and a TH350 in a truck that should have a 700R4. Look for clean grease between the engine and transmission, which suggests nothing has been apart. Check the freeze plugs for weeping.

buying_checks.head: Identify the axles and transfer case
buying_checks.body: On the front axle, a 10-bolt cover is nearly round with no flat sides, while the Dana 44 has the familiar Dana shape. Mismatched gear ratios front and rear, or a missing front driveshaft, mean someone has swapped parts. NP205 and NP203 cases carry ID tags above the front output. On 1989–91 NP241s, a leaking slip-yoke rear output is common.

buying_checks.head: Hubs and 4WD engagement
buying_checks.body: 1981 and later trucks came with automatic locking hubs, which seize with age. One King of the Hammers K5 owner bought a truck with a 'blown transmission' that turned out to be a transfer case stuck in neutral and seized automatic hubs. Engage 4WD on the test drive, and budget for manual hubs.

buying_checks.head: Previous owners' work
buying_checks.body: Look for hacked-in wiring, stereos and lights, cheap lift blocks and poor welding. One CK5 member says to pay extra for a properly done one-ton axle swap (8-lug axles) rather than a cheaply lifted 6-lug truck. Another suggests 1987–91 trucks for fuel injection, with 1989–91 the favorites.

buying_checks.head: M1009 specifics
buying_checks.body: Check whether the 24/12-volt system is original or has been converted. If the resistor pack has been bypassed for 12-volt glow plugs, the starter, the alternator and the NATO slave receptacle in the grille also need dealing with. Expect 3.08 gears, 10.00-15 tires and a governed 55 mph top speed as delivered.

repairs.title: Repair and brace a cracked steering-box frame rail
repairs.time: ≈ A weekend (more if the rail needs welding)
repairs.symptoms: Wandering steering, a box that visibly moves on the frame when someone turns the wheel, or hairline cracks running from the steering-box bolt holes. Big tires and hard wheeling make it worse.
repairs.fix: Unbolt the steering box, swing it aside and clean or blast the rail inside and out, because cracks often show only on the inside. GMSquareBody members drill a stop hole at the end of each crack, gouge it out, weld it, grind it flat, and only then add reinforcement. Offroad Design's weld-on repair kit wraps the outside and bottom of the rail. A bolt-in brace ties the box to the opposite rail and is good insurance on an uncracked frame. Some members also replace loose front-crossmember rivets with grade 8 7/16-inch bolts.
repairs.tools: Welder and grinder · drill and bits · socket set · torque wrench · magnaflux or dye penetrant for hidden cracks

parts.name: Offroad Design weld-on frame repair kit, 1973–91 GM trucks
Offroad Design bolt-in steering box frame brace, 1973–91 4WD

repairs.title: Swap a worn or leaking steering box
repairs.symptoms: Play at the wheel, wandering on the highway, fluid weeping from the box's seals, or a box that has been loosened by a cracking frame.
repairs.fix: Inspect the frame first, because a new box on a cracked rail will soon loosen. Disconnect the steering shaft coupler and the pressure and return lines, pull the pitman arm with a puller, and unbolt the box. Fit the new box with new hardware and a new or rebuilt coupler. Refill and bleed the power steering by turning lock to lock with the front end raised. Lifted trucks often get a dropped pitman arm at the same time to correct drag-link angle.
repairs.tools: Pitman arm puller · flare-nut wrenches · torque wrench · drain pan

parts.name: USA Standard power steering box, 1980–91 4WD GM full-size

repairs.title: Convert seized automatic hubs to manual locking hubs
repairs.symptoms: The truck won't pull with the front wheels in 4WD, grinding from the hubs, or front wheels that drive at one corner only. Automatic locking hubs arrived with the NP208 for 1981 and are now old.
repairs.fix: Raise and support the front, remove the wheel, then remove the automatic hub assembly, its retaining ring and the drag sleeve parts. Check the wheel bearings and the spindle nut adjustment, and repack or replace the bearings if they're dry or rough. Fit the internal-style manual hub kit to suit your axle (10-bolt or Dana 44, spline count). Then check that 2WD and 4WD both engage.
repairs.tools: Snap-ring pliers · spindle nut socket · bearing grease · torque wrench

parts.name: Warn internal-style locking hubs for GM 10-bolt or Dana 44 (all 1/2-ton)
Yukon Hardcore locking hub set, '79+ GM 8.5-in front and Dana 44 (19-spline)

repairs.title: Reseal an NP208 or NP241 and fix a leaking slip yoke
repairs.time: ≈ A day (case out of the truck)
repairs.symptoms: ATF dripping from the rear output, a driveline clunk, or a slip yoke pulling out as the suspension droops on a lifted truck. A worn chain can also skip or slap.
repairs.fix: Both cases are aluminum, chain-driven and filled with ATF. Drain the case, drop both driveshafts and unbolt the case from the transmission adapter. Split the halves, check the chain for stretch and the bearings for wear, and replace all seals and gaskets. On a lifted NP241, a slip-yoke eliminator gives you a fixed rear yoke and a shorter shaft. Offroad Design's kit uses a common 32-spline yoke shortened by 1/4 inch. Refill with ATF.
repairs.tools: Transmission jack · snap-ring pliers · seal drivers · RTV · torque wrench

parts.name: NP241 and NP208 seal and gasket kit
GM NP241 slip yoke eliminator kit

repairs.title: Rebuild the front axle ends (ball joints, U-joints, bearings)
repairs.symptoms: Death-grip steering, clunks over bumps, uneven tire wear, a front end that won't hold alignment, or clicking from the axle U-joints in tight turns in 4WD.
repairs.fix: Identify the axle first. A Dana 44 and a GM 10-bolt look alike, but CK5 members warn that the inner parts and shafts don't interchange. Strip the hubs, calipers and spindles, pull the axle shafts, press out the old U-joints and ball joints, then press in new ones. Replace the spindle bearings and seals, repack the wheel bearings and set the preload. Finish with new hub seals and a front-end alignment.
repairs.tools: Ball joint press · U-joint press or vise · spindle nut socket · slide hammer · torque wrench

parts.name: GM corporate 10-bolt front axle complete rebuild kit

repairs.title: Renew leaf spring bushings and shackles
repairs.symptoms: Clunks, wandering and axle wrap. Sagging rear springs are also common, and cracked rubber bushings often squeak.
repairs.fix: Support the frame and take the weight off one spring at a time. Unbolt the shackle and main-eye bolts, press out the old bushings, and fit new ones that match your springs, since stock and aftermarket lift springs use different bushings. Fit greasable heavy-duty front shackles while you're there. Torque everything with the truck on the ground at ride height. Offroad Design publishes a chart of which bushing fits each stock or aftermarket spring.
repairs.tools: Jack stands · bushing press or vise · penetrating oil · torque wrench

parts.name: Universal 1969–91 full-vehicle bushing kit with HD front shackles
Rear main-eye leaf spring hanger for 1981–91 4WD K5 Blazer/Jimmy

repairs.title: 6.2 diesel glow plugs and controller
repairs.symptoms: Hard cold starts, long cranking, white smoke until warm, or a wait light that misbehaves. On an M1009, a bad resistor pack or a mixed 12/24-volt conversion can cook new plugs.
repairs.fix: Test each glow plug's resistance and check that power reaches each one during the glow cycle. Replace failed plugs (or all eight) and the controller or relay if it isn't cycling. On M1009s, confirm whether the truck still has the 24-volt starting system and the firewall resistor pack before you buy plugs. The plugs are 12-volt even on CUCVs, and the resistor pack drops 24 volts to 12.
repairs.tools: Multimeter · deep sockets and extensions · anti-seize

baseline_service.intro: Assume nothing has been done. These trucks are 35 to 50 years old, and most have had several owners and swaps. Before you buy fluids, identify the engine, transmission, transfer case and axles, since they changed every few years. Pull the steering box and look at the frame while you're under there. Capacities vary by drivetrain, so check them in the factory manual.

items.note: Look for leaks at the rear main seal and the oil pan.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: About 32 inches. Hogback Fabrication says on CK5 that a stock K5 fits 32s without trimming and 33s with minor trimming. Other owners report 33s rubbing the inner fender at full lock and full bump, but fine on the road. On 16-inch wheels, 285/75R16s are commonly said not to rub. Wheel width and backspacing matter: one member suggests 15x8 wheels at about 3.5 inches of backspacing as the easy fit for 33x12.50s.

faq.q: Which years should I look for?
faq.a: It depends on what you want. The 1973–75 trucks have the fully open body, which MotorTrend calls the K5's sweet spot for that reason, and 1976–80 trucks are the classic half-cab with the NP205 or NP203 and simpler mechanicals. For a truck to drive, CK5 owners mostly point to the 1987–91 trucks for throttle-body injection, and many name 1989–91 as the best of those for the NP241 transfer case, 30-spline axle shafts and the updated 700R4. Others prefer 1990–91 for the electronic speedometer. Whatever the year, check the frame at the steering box.

faq.q: Does mine have a Dana 44 or a 10-bolt front axle?
faq.a: Look at the cover. Torque King describes the GM 10-bolt cover as an oval about 11 by 10-1/4 inches with no flat sides, unlike the Dana 44's. 1973–76 half-tons used the Dana 44, 1977–78 trucks could have either, and from 1979 Blazers used the 10-bolt through 1991, according to one GMSquareBody member's list (another CK5 member says GMC used up its last Dana 44s through 1982). Thirty-spline 10-bolt shafts came in around 1989.

faq.q: Which transfer case do I have?
faq.a: Up to 1980 you'll find the gear-driven NP205, a one-piece iron case with a small three-bolt idler cover on the back, or the full-time NP203, a long four-section case with a separate range box on the front. From 1981 the aluminum, chain-driven NP208 took over, and the NP241 replaced it from 1989. The 208 and 241 both take ATF.

It's slow but simple. At launch it made 130 hp and 240 lb-ft, with a mechanical injection pump and indirect injection, and it fits the same mounts as the gas V8. Known problems include cracked main-bearing webs, and crank failures linked to worn harmonic balancers. Inspect the balancer and find out the engine's history before you buy.

It's a 1983–87 Army K5 with the 6.2 diesel, a TH400 and an NP208, 10-bolt axles with 3.08 gears and an Eaton automatic rear locker, heavier springs and 10.00-15 tires. It has a 24/12-volt electrical system and is rated for 1,200 lb of payload and 3,000 lb towed. GM built about 70,000 CUCVs of all types.

faq.q: How does the removable top work?
faq.a: On 1973–75 trucks the whole roof behind the windshield came off, with a hardtop or a convertible top. From 1976 the front roof is steel and fixed, and only the fiberglass rear top unbolts. That stayed true through 1991. Offroad Design still sells a soft top for 1969–91 K5s and Jimmys.

faq.q: How good is the fuel economy?
faq.a: Bad with a gas V8. Popular Science's 1973 test of a 350 automatic with full-time 4WD recorded 9.6 mpg at a steady 45 mph. A 1974 250 six with an automatic managed 13.7 mpg at the same speed. Offroad Design got 11–12 mpg on a road trip in its lifted 1988 TBI Suburban, which has the same drivetrain.

faq.q: What gears do I need for bigger tires?
faq.a: More than you'd think. Offroad Design put 4.56 one-ton axles under its 1988 Suburban, with a TBI 350, a 700R4 and 35-inch tires, and found it had enough rpm but still not enough power. On CK5, one member recommends at least 4.56 for 38s and 5.13s for 35-inch-and-up tires on one-ton axles. M1009s left the factory with tall 3.08s.

faq.q: Can I put one-ton axles under it?
faq.a: Yes. A Dana 60 front and 14-bolt rear from a K30 is the classic upgrade. CK5 members note that the K30's rear spring pads sit about 2 inches narrower than the Blazer's, and the perches and shock tabs need moving. Driveshaft lengths change too. The bigger brakes may also need a larger master cylinder.

Prices vary a lot. Bring a Trailer's 15 most recent K5 sales (August–October 2026) ran from $4,600 for a 1986 project to $130,000 for an LSA-powered 1973, with a median of $29,500. Stock trucks mostly sold for $15,000–38,500, and a 1984 M1009 sold for $20,500. Hagerty noted in 2019 that the Blazer's median #2-condition value had risen 164% since 2009.

The Army rated the M1009 for a 3,000 lb towed load. Wikipedia says the six-cylinder Blazer wasn't recommended for towing. For a civilian truck, go by the GVWR, axle ratio and hitch it actually has, and check the factory trailering guide for your year.
